comparison: Both evaluate the MLG reconstruction methodology (C3, C57, C146-C147). OpenEval finds the approach clearly described and well-supported. Peer reviewers also support the reconstruction, with the first reviewer noting 'solid estimation of syntenic relationships' though the second reviewer questions the ancestral chromosome number optimization methodology.

Both address translocation rate analysis (C114, C148). OpenEval finds the methods clear and results important for showing chiton rearrangement isn't due to higher translocation rates. Peer reviewer questions whether the data presentation justifies broader claims, noting the summary tables don't adequately separate taxa by age, making mean values 'not especially helpful.'

Both evaluate the partial genome duplication in L. japonica (C7-C8, C77, C109-C110). OpenEval finds the evidence well-supported by figures and logical inference. Peer reviewers do not challenge this specific finding, treating it as an accepted observation from the genomic analysis.

Both address heterozygosity findings (C52, C120, C122). OpenEval finds these supported by genomic data and appropriate comparative context. Peer reviewers also accept these as quality metrics and observations without dispute.

Both evaluate the finding of maximum genomic rearrangement in morphologically conservative Lepidopleurida (C6, C71, C74). OpenEval finds this a well-supported key finding that challenges assumptions. Peer reviewers do not challenge this specific observation.

Both address ancestral state reconstruction findings (C78-C80). OpenEval finds these directly supported by comparative analysis. Peer reviewer raises serious methodological concerns about ancestral reconstruction, questioning how they arrived at 16 ancestral chromosomes when no chiton has more than 13, and criticizing the lack of proper outgroup usage.

Both evaluate genome duplication findings across Mollusca (C106-C107, C111). OpenEval finds these confirmatory results strengthen confidence in the approach. Peer reviewers also accept these findings without challenge as confirmatory results from comparative analysis.

Both address phylogenetic analysis and results (C53-C56). OpenEval finds methods appropriate with results consistent with prior work. Peer reviewers treat phylogenetic findings as confirmatory rather than controversial, with the first reviewer noting the study provides 'an update for how these relate to molluscan genomes.'

Both evaluate MLG conservation in bivalves (C4, C94, C97, C99). OpenEval finds this well-supported and providing important context. Peer reviewer acknowledges conservation in bivalves is not disputed, noting 'Perhaps it is safest to conclude that these MLGs are mostly conserved in conchiferans.'

Both address extreme genomic rearrangement claims in chitons (C5, C59, C65, C129-C130). OpenEval finds the characterization as 'almost unprecedented' well-supported by extensive comparative data. Peer reviewer expresses significant doubt, stating 'I still am unconvinced by the authors' claims to have demonstrated an unusually high rate' and questions whether the amount is 'especially rapid or slow,' though acknowledges impressive rearrangements within Acanthochitona.

Both evaluate major conclusions about extreme rearrangement and morphological conservation (C9-C11). OpenEval finds these well-supported by extensive genomic data contrasted with morphological conservation. Peer reviewer directly challenges these claims, stating they are 'unconvinced' the data 'justify the implications of the title or the claims made in the Summary' and noting insufficient justification that the pace is 'in any way remarkable.'

Both evaluate genomic data generation and quality (C2, C41-C42, C49-C51). OpenEval finds methods clearly described with high quality assemblies. Peer reviewers strongly support this, with the first reviewer stating this is an 'important study' that has 'nearly doubled the number of genome sequences for chitons' with 'very well annotated' genomes, and the second reviewer acknowledging 'substantial' contributions.

OpenEval evaluates extreme genomic variation within Acanthochitona genus (C66-C70). Peer reviewer R4 addresses broader rearrangement claims including some Acanthochitona data (C67, C70). OpenEval finds the within-genus variation well-documented. Peer reviewer acknowledges 'impressive rearrangements within Acanthochitona' but questions the broader comparative context.
